Six Trademark Clauses Every China OEM Agreement Needs

A Chinese OEM relationship is also a trademark exposure. China is a first-to-file jurisdiction, and the factory that prints your logo knows your launch date, your volumes and your designs. The inexpensive protection is not a lawsuit after registration; it is six clauses agreed before the first purchase order.

Why the Factory Is a Trademark Risk

China generally awards trademark rights to the party that files first, not the party that used the mark first. A contract manufacturer sits at the worst possible point in that system: it receives your artwork, sees your seasonal volumes, knows which classes you have not covered, and can file before your own application is even prepared. Article 20 of the revised Trademark Law refuses marks identical or similar to an earlier registered or applied-for mark, Article 24 protects prior legitimate rights and addresses bad-faith squatting, and Article 19 allows refusal of applications filed with no intention to use that clearly exceed normal business needs.

Those provisions are a remedy, not a plan. Invoking them means opposition or invalidation proceedings, evidence of your reputation, and a period during which the factory holds a registration that can block your own filing or disrupt a platform listing. A well-drafted agreement moves the fight forward to a signature and turns a dispute about ownership into a simple breach of contract.

The six clauses below come from standard practitioner guidance on China manufacturing agreements. They are not exotic. What makes them work is specificity: a named right, a measurable quantity, a deadline, and a consequence that a court or arbitration panel can actually apply. Generic language about protecting intellectual property is close to worthless once a dispute starts.

Register first, contract second. A contract binds your counterparty; a registration binds the world. File your Latin and Chinese-character marks in the relevant classes before production begins, then use the agreement to close the gaps a registration cannot reach.

Clauses 1 to 2: Ownership and Volume Control

Clause 1 is a registration ban with teeth. Prohibit the factory, its affiliates and its subcontractors from applying to register the brand, the Chinese name, the logo, the product shape or any confusingly similar variant in any jurisdiction, and require the factory to assign to you, at its own cost, any mark it has registered in breach. Add a liquidated-damages clause and a duty to cooperate in withdrawal, opposition or invalidation. Without the assignment obligation and the penalty, a ban is a promise with no remedy attached.

Clause 2 caps production. Authorise a maximum quantity per order and per period, require periodic reconciliation of purchase orders against finished goods, and reserve an audit right over production records, scrap and dispatch logs. The clause most drafters omit is the adverse inference: where the records cannot explain a quantity of branded goods, that quantity is treated as unauthorised production. This shifts the evidentiary burden to the party that holds the factory data.

ClauseRight createdConsequence if breached
1. Registration banNo filing by the factory or its affiliates; compulsory assignment of any mark obtained in breachLiquidated damages plus a duty to cooperate in withdrawal or transfer
2. Volume capFixed authorised quantity, reconciliation and audit of recordsUnexplained quantities presumed unauthorised; breach of contract

Clauses 3 to 4: Quality Control and the Exit Plan

Clause 3 gives you sampling and inspection rights over production runs, packaging and printed materials, and states what happens when a batch fails: rejection, rework at the factory's cost, supervised destruction of defective branded goods, and suspension of further shipments. Quality control is not only about consumer safety. Uncontrolled use by a manufacturer can weaken a mark, and goods bearing your mark that you never approved are difficult to disown later.

Clause 4 is the exit plan, and it is where most disputes actually start. When the relationship ends, the factory may still hold finished stock, work in progress, moulds, tooling, plates, labels and packaging. Deal with each category separately and set a deadline for every one of them: sell-off of approved finished stock within a defined window, destruction or buy-back of semi-finished goods, and surrender or destruction of moulds and printing plates. Silence on these items is an invitation for a former supplier to keep producing.

Tie the exit clause to a short written handover checklist and a final reconciliation of quantities, so that ownership of every remaining branded item is recorded while the relationship is still cooperative rather than during a dispute.

Clauses 5 to 6: Secrecy and Channel Allocation

Clause 5 covers the material the factory receives: design artwork, specifications, mould files, packaging artwork, supplier lists and customer lists. Require confidentiality, restrict use to performing the specific order, prohibit disclosure to subcontractors without written approval, and state expressly that the duty survives termination. Survival language matters because the leak usually happens after the last order, when the factory markets a near-identical product to a new client.

Clause 6 allocates responsibility for where the goods go. Separate export and domestic channels: state which party may sell into the Chinese market, which party handles platform authorisations and customs or regulatory records, and who bears liability if branded goods appear in an unauthorised channel. This is also where the trademark chain is documented, since a domestic sale by the factory is the fact pattern that most often turns a supplier into a squatter.

Do not rely on the contract alone. Record licences where required, keep dated use evidence, and watch the register for filings by the factory or its affiliates. Articles 55 and 57 of the revised law address licence recordal and cancellation of unused marks; a contract that is never reflected in your portfolio leaves gaps a filing can exploit.

From Contract to Portfolio

The agreement should sit inside a broader filing and monitoring routine rather than replace it. Before the first production run, file the Latin word mark and the Chinese-character mark as separate applications: in China these are separate rights, and a registration for one does not cover the other. Cover the classes you sell in and the classes a supplier or squatter is likely to target, and consider separate applications for the device element rather than one combined mark.

Then operationalise the clauses. Put a named owner on the quantity reconciliation, keep the audit right exercisable on notice, diary the post-termination stock deadlines, and run a watch over the register and major marketplaces for filings or listings by the factory, its affiliates and its directors. Where a licence relationship exists, keep it documented so that use by the licensee can be proved.

When a supplier does file, treat the contract as evidence, not as a shield: the registration ban, the assignment duty and the documented relationship all strengthen a bad-faith case, but the timetable starts from the publication or filing date, not from the date you discover the problem. Decide in advance who is authorised to instruct local counsel, because the short statutory windows leave no time for a fresh internal approval chain. Sources and Caveats

Basis: practitioner guidance on trademark clauses in China OEM and manufacturing agreements; Articles 19, 20, 24, 55 and 57 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (adopted 26 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027). The clause list reflects general industry practice, not a prescribed statutory form; have the agreement reviewed under the law governing the contract. Procedures and official practice may be refined by revised implementing regulations and examination guidelines, so confirm the current official announcements and rules with your adviser. This is general information, not legal advice.
